questions.prompt: Where does `InlineArray` store its elements?

options.text: Inline on the stack or directly inside its parent type.
options.explanation: Right. InlineArray stores elements inline without its own heap buffer or ARC overhead.

options.text: Always in a shared heap buffer with copy-on-write.
options.explanation: Wrong. That describes standard Array, not InlineArray.

options.text: In a separate heap buffer managed by reference counting.
options.explanation: Wrong. InlineArray does not allocate its own heap buffer or use ARC.

options.text: On the heap only when the count exceeds three items.
options.explanation: Wrong. Every InlineArray stores its elements inline regardless of count.

questions.prompt: What is the shorthand type syntax for `InlineArray<3, Int>` in Swift?

options.text: [Int * 3]
options.explanation: Wrong. Swift uses [3 of Int], not [Int * 3].

options.text: [3 of Int]
options.explanation: Right. [count of Element] is the shorthand syntax for InlineArray.

options.text: Array<Int, 3>
options.explanation: Wrong. Array only takes one generic Element parameter and grows dynamically.

options.text: (Int, Int, Int)[]
options.explanation: Wrong. That is not valid Swift syntax.

questions.prompt: Can you call `append` to grow an `InlineArray` at runtime?

options.text: Yes, if you declare it with var.
options.explanation: Wrong. Even with var, the element count is fixed in the type.

options.text: Yes, up to twice its initial capacity.
options.explanation: Wrong. InlineArray never resizes or reallocates.

options.text: No, its count is fixed at compile time.
options.explanation: Right. [3 of Int] always holds exactly 3 elements and cannot grow or shrink.

options.text: Only when the element count is inferred with _.
options.explanation: Wrong. Type inference still fixes the count at compile time, so append is not available.

questions.prompt: What is a `Span<Element>` in Swift?

options.text: An owning dynamic list that grows on the heap.
options.explanation: Wrong. Span does not own memory and cannot resize.

options.text: An unsafe raw pointer with no bounds checks.
options.explanation: Wrong. Span checks index bounds and enforces lifetime safety.

options.text: A copy-on-write slice that allocates when mutated.
options.explanation: Wrong. Span does not own memory or use copy-on-write.

options.text: A non-owning, read-only, safe view over contiguous memory.
options.explanation: Right. Span lets functions read contiguous elements without copying or unsafe pointers.

questions.prompt: What two safety guarantees does `Span` provide over `UnsafeBufferPointer`?

options.text: Spatial bounds checking and temporal lifetime checking.
options.explanation: Right. Span checks index bounds and prevents outliving the container it borrows.

options.text: Automatic heap allocation and copy-on-write buffering.
options.explanation: Wrong. Span does not allocate heap memory or own buffers.

options.text: Automatic thread locking and optional index lookups.
options.explanation: Wrong. Span does not lock threads, and subscripting returns an Element directly.

options.text: Implicit nil fallback on out-of-range subscripts.
options.explanation: Wrong. Out-of-bounds subscripting traps safely rather than returning nil.

questions.prompt: Which property on a `Span` gives you a bounds-checked `RawSpan` over its bytes?

options.text: .unsafePointer
options.explanation: Wrong. Span avoids exposing raw unsafe pointers by default.

options.text: .bytes
options.explanation: Right. Accessing span.bytes produces a RawSpan for safe byte inspection.

options.text: .heapCopy
options.explanation: Wrong. Span does not copy elements to the heap.

options.text: .rawBuffer
options.explanation: Wrong. The property on Span is named bytes.

questions.prompt: Which span type is used to safely initialize uninitialized elements when building a new `Array`?

options.text: RawSpan
options.explanation: Wrong. RawSpan provides read-only access to raw bytes.

options.text: MutableSpan
options.explanation: Wrong. MutableSpan edits already-initialized elements in place.

options.text: OutputSpan
options.explanation: Right. OutputSpan tracks initialized vs uninitialized slots safely via append.

options.text: MutableRawSpan
options.explanation: Wrong. MutableRawSpan edits already-initialized raw bytes, not uninitialized Element slots.

questions.prompt: How does copying an `InlineArray` compare to copying a standard `Array`?

options.text: InlineArray uses copy-on-write on the heap just like Array.
options.explanation: Wrong. InlineArray has no heap buffer, so it cannot use copy-on-write.

options.text: InlineArray shares a reference so mutating the copy changes the original.
options.explanation: Wrong. InlineArray is a value type; mutating the copy leaves the original unchanged.

options.text: InlineArray cannot be assigned to another variable at all.
options.explanation: Wrong. When Element is Copyable, InlineArray can be copied on assignment.

options.text: InlineArray copies all elements eagerly on assignment instead of using copy-on-write.
options.explanation: Right. Because elements sit inline, assigning var b = a copies every element right away.

questions.prompt: Can `InlineArray` store `~Copyable` (noncopyable) elements?

options.text: Yes, InlineArray supports ~Copyable element types.
options.explanation: Right. InlineArray supports noncopyable elements without forcing Copyable.

options.text: No, InlineArray requires Element to conform to Copyable.
options.explanation: Wrong. InlineArray explicitly supports ~Copyable elements.

options.text: Only if the element count is 1.
options.explanation: Wrong. Any fixed compile-time count works with ~Copyable elements.

options.text: Only inside an unsafe pointer block.
options.explanation: Wrong. Structs and enums that are ~Copyable work directly inside InlineArray.

questions.prompt: What does `~Escapable` mean on `Span`?

options.text: The Span cannot contain escaping closures.
options.explanation: Wrong. ~Escapable refers to the Span value's own lifetime, not closures.

options.text: The Span cannot outlive the scope or owner it borrows memory from.
options.explanation: Right. Non-escapable lifetime rules stop a Span from becoming a dangling view.

options.text: The Span automatically copies its elements when returned from a function.
options.explanation: Wrong. Returning a Span from a local variable is a compile error.

options.text: The Span disables Swift 6 Sendable checking.
options.explanation: Wrong. ~Escapable tracks lifetime bounds, not concurrency.

questions.prompt: Why does Swift reject keeping `fixed.span` alive while taking `fixed.mutableSpan` in the same scope?

options.text: Because InlineArray allows only one span over its whole lifetime.
options.explanation: Wrong. You can use both sequentially in separate scopes.

options.text: Because MutableSpan converts InlineArray into a class.
options.explanation: Wrong. InlineArray remains a value type.

options.text: Mutating requires exclusive access, so Span and MutableSpan cannot overlap.
options.explanation: Right. Swift enforces exclusive access so no reader observes mid-mutation memory.

options.text: Because Span is always heap-allocated and locks the main thread.
options.explanation: Wrong. Span has no heap allocation or thread lock.

questions.prompt: Which parameter style avoids copying a huge `[1024 of Int]` when calling a read-only helper function?

options.text: Pass it by value to a normal parameter.
options.explanation: Wrong. Passing a large InlineArray by value can copy all 1024 integers.

options.text: Copy it into a standard Array before calling.
options.explanation: Wrong. Converting to Array allocates on the heap and copies all elements.

options.text: Mark the parameter @escaping in the function.
options.explanation: Wrong. @escaping applies to closures, not InlineArray parameters.

options.text: Pass .span (or mark the parameter borrowing).
options.explanation: Right. Passing .span or borrowing avoids copying the inline elements.

questions.prompt: Why can a single function taking `Span<Int>` work on both `Array<Int>` and `[3 of Int]`?

options.text: Both Array and InlineArray expose .span over their contiguous storage.
options.explanation: Right. Span abstracts over contiguous memory without caring which container owns it.

options.text: Because InlineArray is a subclass of Array.
options.explanation: Wrong. Both are structs and structs cannot inherit.

options.text: Because Span copies both inputs into a new Array.
options.explanation: Wrong. Span borrows existing contiguous storage with zero copies.

options.text: Because Array and InlineArray conform to AnyObject.
options.explanation: Wrong. Neither is a class.

questions.prompt: When should you stick with `Array` instead of switching to `InlineArray`?

options.text: Only when targeting iOS 12.
options.explanation: Wrong. Array is the default choice across all iOS versions.

options.text: For general code where the count varies or heap overhead is not a bottleneck.
options.explanation: Right. Array handles dynamic sizes and copy-on-write well for normal app logic.

options.text: Never; InlineArray should replace every Array in Swift 6.
options.explanation: Wrong. InlineArray has fixed size and eager copying, so it only fits specific hot paths.

options.text: Only when storing String values.
options.explanation: Wrong. InlineArray can store String too, if count is fixed.

questions.prompt: What happens if you put a huge `[1024 of Int]` directly inside a `struct` that is copied often?

options.text: Swift automatically moves it to the heap with copy-on-write.
options.explanation: Wrong. InlineArray stays inline inside the parent struct.

options.text: Only a 1-word pointer is copied when the struct is assigned.
options.explanation: Wrong. All inline elements live directly inside the struct layout.

options.text: Every copy of that struct copies all 1024 integers eagerly.
options.explanation: Right. InlineArray grows the parent struct size and copies eagerly on every value copy.

options.text: The compiler turns the struct into a class automatically.
options.explanation: Wrong. Swift never silently changes a struct into a class.

questions.prompt: Why is `OutputSpan` safer than `Array.init(unsafeUninitializedCapacity:)`?

options.text: OutputSpan disables bounds checks for maximum speed.
options.explanation: Wrong. OutputSpan tracks initialized elements safely with bounds checks.

options.text: OutputSpan fills every unused slot with nil automatically.
options.explanation: Wrong. OutputSpan only initializes the elements you append.

options.text: OutputSpan lets you read uninitialized slots safely as zero.
options.explanation: Wrong. OutputSpan separates initialized items from uninitialized space and tracks the count.

options.text: OutputSpan tracks initialized count automatically without raw pointer math.
options.explanation: Right. You append safely instead of managing raw pointers and manual initializedCount integers.

questions.prompt: In 2–5 sentences, explain how `InlineArray` differs from a standard `Array` in storage and copying behavior.

rubric.criterion: States that InlineArray stores a compile-time fixed count inline without heap allocation or ARC
States that Array allocates on the heap with copy-on-write and can resize
Explains that InlineArray copies all elements eagerly on assignment instead of using copy-on-write

questions.modelAnswer: Standard Array stores elements in a resizable heap buffer with reference counting and copy-on-write. InlineArray has a compile-time fixed size and stores its elements inline on the stack or inside a parent type with zero heap allocation. Because there is no shared heap buffer, InlineArray copies all elements eagerly on assignment.

questions.prompt: In 2–5 sentences, explain what `Span` is and how it prevents both out-of-bounds reads and dangling-pointer bugs.

rubric.criterion: Explains spatial safety: every subscript access on Span is bounds-checked
Explains temporal safety: Span is ~Escapable so the compiler makes sure it cannot outlive its owner
Notes that Span is a non-owning view with zero heap allocation

questions.modelAnswer: Span is a non-owning view over contiguous memory that adds zero heap allocations. For spatial safety, every subscript access checks bounds so code cannot read past the end of the buffer. For temporal safety, Span is ~Escapable, meaning the compiler prevents returning or storing it past the owner's lifetime.

questions.prompt: In 2–5 sentences, describe the roles of `Span`, `MutableSpan`, `RawSpan`, and `OutputSpan`.

rubric.criterion: Identifies Span as read-only and MutableSpan as exclusive in-place mutable view
Identifies RawSpan as a bounds-checked raw bytes view
Identifies OutputSpan as a safe helper for initializing uninitialized buffers

questions.modelAnswer: Span provides a read-only, bounds-checked view over typed contiguous elements, while MutableSpan gives exclusive write access to mutate elements in place. RawSpan (via .bytes) exposes a safe, bounds-checked view of raw bytes. OutputSpan safely initializes new memory slots, such as inside Array(capacity:), without raw pointer math.

questions.prompt: In 2–5 sentences, explain the risk of passing a large `InlineArray` by value and two ways to avoid copying it.

rubric.criterion: Explains that InlineArray lacks copy-on-write, so passing by value copies all elements eagerly
States passing .span or marking the parameter borrowing avoids copying

questions.modelAnswer: Because InlineArray stores elements inline with no copy-on-write buffer, passing a large InlineArray by value copies every element eagerly. To avoid those copies, pass its .span into functions that accept Span. You can also mark the function parameter as borrowing so Swift lends the value without copying.

questions.prompt: In 2–5 sentences, explain when a team should choose `Array`, `InlineArray`, or `Span` in a real iOS app.

rubric.criterion: Recommends Array as the default when sizes vary or allocations are not a bottleneck
Recommends InlineArray when profiling shows heap or ARC overhead for small fixed-size buffers
Recommends Span at function or API boundaries so functions accept any contiguous storage with zero copies

questions.modelAnswer: Use Array as your default collection for UI state and lists where size changes at runtime. Switch to InlineArray when Instruments shows heap or ARC overhead on small, fixed-size buffers like audio frames. Use Span in helper functions so one API can read Array or InlineArray data with zero copies.
